findings.title: Raw recovery codes are handed to the user-storage provider; the user label is dropped
findings.body: On the local path only hashes are persisted, via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`. The new user-storage path serializes the unhashed `generatedCodes` to JSON and passes them in a `UserCredentialModel` to `updateCredential`. The external provider (and anything it logs or stores) therefore receives usable one-time bypass credentials in clear text. The user-supplied label (`generatedUserLabel`) is also silently discarded on this path. This difference from local storage should at least be documented, and ideally the provider should receive the hashed credential data rather than raw codes.

findings.title: Existing local recovery codes are not removed when the user storage accepts the new codes
findings.body: When `updateCredential` returns true, the method only logs and never touches an existing locally stored recovery-codes credential. `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` prefers the federated credential, but a user who previously had local codes keeps a stale hashed credential in the Keycloak DB. That credential still counts for `isConfiguredFor` and credential listings. It also becomes active again if the storage provider later stops supporting the type. The local credential should be removed or replaced when the storage takes over.

findings.title: Exhausted-code cleanup and next-code lookup do not work for federated credentials
findings.body: `getCredential` can now return a credential that came from user storage. The code that follows was written for locally stored credentials. When `allCodesUsed()` is true it calls `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, but a federated credential may have a null or non-local id (the test storage's `getCredentials` returns a model with no id). That call does not remove the credential from the storage, so the exhausted credential stays and is still returned first on the next login. `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` then calls `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` on an empty Optional and throws `NoSuchElementException`, which breaks the login page. There is also no step that records a used code in the federated store, so single-use semantics depend entirely on the provider. None of this is handled or tested.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser
findings.body: `getMyUser(user)` returns null when the user is not in the map, for example after `removeUser`. `getCredentials` then does `myUser.recoveryCodes` and throws an NPE. The neighbouring methods `isConfiguredFor` and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` guard against null. Since `getFederatedCredentialsStream` now routes through this method, a missing user should yield an empty stream. In addition, the returned recovery-codes model has no id, so account credential listings and any `removeStoredCredentialById` call would see a null id.

findings.title: Recovery-keys test covers only the happy path and hides that codes are never consumed
findings.body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once with code index 0. It has no negative case (wrong code rejected), no check that a used code is consumed or that the next login asks for index 1, and no check that a user with local credentials still works through the fallback. The test storage's `isValid` never marks codes as used, so the same code is accepted forever, and the prompted index would stay 0. The test therefore passes without exercising the single-use behaviour. The extra `delayed-authenticator` sub-flow, with a typo'd alias "delayed-suthenticator-config" and a delay of 0, adds nothing to what is being tested.
